title: Chapter 51 — The Spirit-Spout
paragraphs: Days, weeks passed, and under easy sail, the ivory Pequod had slowly swept across four separate cruising-grounds: the one off the Azores, the one off the Cape Verdes, the Plate — so called because it lies off the mouth of the Rio de la Plata — and the Carrol Ground, an unmarked watery expanse south of St. Helena.

It was while gliding through these last waters that one serene and moonlit night, when all the waves rolled by like scrolls of silver, and by their soft, spreading murmur made what seemed a silvery silence rather than a solitude — on such a silent night a silvery jet was seen far ahead of the white bubbles at the bow. Lit up by the moon, it looked celestial — like some plumed and glittering god rising from the sea. Fedallah first spotted this jet. For on these moonlit nights, it was his habit to climb to the main masthead and stand lookout there with the same precision as if it had been day. And the crew would find him there in the morning, still standing in the same posture, his fixed gaze aimed at the same advancing point. No matter how still the night, his thin lips moved on and on, as if muttering some endless prayer.

Walking the deck with quick, side-lunging strides, Ahab ordered the topgallant sails and royals set, and every studding-sail spread. The best helmsman on the ship was put at the wheel. Then, with every masthead manned, the loaded ship rolled down before the wind. The strange uplifting force of the stern breeze filling the hollows of so many sails made the buoyant, hovering deck feel like air beneath the feet. Still she rushed along, as if two opposing forces struggled within her — one to soar straight to heaven, the other to drive her toward some horizontal goal. And all the while the phantom jet kept rising ahead.

This midnight spout had almost become a forgotten thing when, some days later — there it was again: at the same silent hour, announced again, spotted by all. But when we set sail to overtake it, it once more vanished as if it had never existed. And so it served us night after night, until no one paid it any attention except to marvel at it. Mysteriously thrown into the clear moonlight or starlight, disappearing again for one, two, or three whole days, and somehow seeming at every new appearance to be advancing still further ahead of us — this solitary jet seemed forever beckoning us on.

Nor, given the ancient superstition of their race and the supernatural aura that seemed in many ways to surround the Pequod, were there lacking some seamen who swore that whenever and wherever that spout appeared — however far apart in time and place — it was cast by one and the same whale: Moby Dick. For a time, there also reigned a sense of peculiar dread at this flitting apparition, as if it were treacherously beckoning us on and on so that the monster might turn around upon us and tear us apart at last in some remote and savage sea.

These temporary fears, so vague but so awful, drew a strange power from the contrasting calm of the weather. Beneath all its blue gentleness, some thought there lurked a devilish charm, as for days upon days we voyaged through seas so wearily, so lonesomely mild that all of space, repelled by our vengeful mission, seemed to be emptying itself of life before our funeral-urn prow.

But at last, when we turned eastward, the Cape winds began howling around us, and we rose and fell upon the long, troubled seas that lie there. When the ivory-tusked Pequod bowed sharply to the blast and drove into the dark waves in her fury, until showers of silver chips — the foam-flakes — flew over her bulwarks, then all this desolate emptiness of life went away, but gave place to sights more dismal than before.

Close to our bow, strange shapes darted back and forth in the water before us, while thick behind us flew inscrutable sea-ravens. Every morning, perched on our rigging, rows of these birds were seen. Despite our shouting, they stubbornly clung to the ropes for a long time, as though they considered our ship some drifting, uninhabited craft — a thing fated for desolation, and therefore a fitting roosting-place for their homeless selves. And the black sea heaved and heaved, still relentlessly heaving, as if its vast tides were a conscience, and the great soul of the world were in anguish and remorse for the long sin and suffering it had caused.

Cape of Good Hope, do they call you? Rather Cape Tormentoso, as they named you long ago. For long deceived by the treacherous silences that had attended us before, we found ourselves launched into this tormented sea, where guilty beings transformed into those birds and those fish seemed condemned to swim forever without any harbor in store, or to beat that black air without any horizon. But calm, snow-white, and unchanging — still directing its fountain of feathers toward the sky — still beckoning us on from ahead — the solitary jet would at times appear.

During all this blackness of the elements, Ahab, though taking near-constant command of the drenched and dangerous deck, showed the gloomiest reserve and spoke to his mates less often than ever. In storms like these, after everything above and aloft has been secured, nothing more can be done but passively await the outcome of the gale. Then Captain and crew become practical fatalists. So, with his ivory leg inserted into its usual hole and with one hand firmly gripping a shroud, Ahab would stand for hours gazing dead to windward, while an occasional sleet or snow would drive against him and plaster itself upon his coat. Meanwhile, the Pequod would sometimes roll so fiercely that an icicle formed on one side of the helmsman's tiller would be dipped into the sea on the other. But even though drenched to the bone and half-frozen, Ahab stubbornly refused to seek shelter in the cabin, for its floor was one that he could not bear. It was dangerous enough for him to navigate any ship's deck in rough weather. But to stand on the Pequod's cabin floor was worse than standing on the backs of wild bulls. And so it was that one night, his ivory leg having received a sharp blow, he was hurled heavily against the deck. From then on, a watchman — whose task was to attend to the cabin lamp and binnacle — was stationed at the cabin door. The binnacle is called the tell-tale, because without going to the compass at the helm, the Captain, while below, can read the ship's course from his berth.
The cabin-compass is called the tell-tale because without going to the compass at the helm, the Captain, while below, can read the ship's course.
Terrible old man! thought Starbuck with a shudder. Sleeping through this gale, still you steadfastly keep your eye on your purpose.
